claim: ERK3 protein levels steadily decrease during epithelial differentiation in mouse colon organoids (MCOs).
source: ERK3 protein levels are significantly lower in the differentiated MCOs as compared to the undifferentiated ones (Figure 1C–D).
evidence: The claim is supported by western blot data (Figure 1C) and quantification (Figure 1D) showing decreased ERK3 protein in differentiated vs undifferentiated MCOs.

claim: ERK3 mRNA levels are slightly higher in differentiated mouse colon organoids compared to undifferentiated ones.
source: The mRNA levels of Erk3 were slightly higher under differentiated conditions (Figure 1E).
evidence: RT-PCR data in Figure 1E shows increased Erk3 mRNA in differentiated MCOs.

claim: The decrease in ERK3 expression in differentiated MCOs is regulated at the protein level.
source: Taken together, these data suggest that the decrease in ERK3 expression observed in the differentiated MCOs is regulated at the protein levels.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that protein levels decrease while mRNA levels increase during differentiation.

claim: ERK3 protein levels steadily decrease during the differentiation of human gastric organoids (HGOs).
source: ERK3 protein levels steadily decrease during the differentiation of HGOs without much change in the mRNA levels (Figure 1F–I, Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Western blot analysis (Figure 1F-H) and RT-PCR (Figure 1I) demonstrate decreasing ERK3 protein but stable mRNA during HGO differentiation.

claim: LPS stimulation leads to a time-dependent increase in ERK3 protein levels in HT-29 cells.
source: LPS stimulation led to a time-dependent increase in the protein levels of ERK3 with concomitant increase in the phosphorylation status of S189 during the time frame of the experiment (Figure 2A and B).
evidence: Western blot data (Figure 2A) and quantification (Figure 2B) show increased ERK3 protein and phosphorylation in HT-29 cells after LPS treatment.

claim: LPS stimulation does not change ERK4 protein levels in HT-29 cells.
source: We did not detect any changes in the protein levels of the closely related MAPK ERK4 (MAPK4) (Figure 2A).
evidence: Western blot in Figure 2A shows stable ERK4 levels across LPS treatment time points.

claim: MK5 is activated in response to LPS in HT-29 cells.
source: MK5 (MAPKAPK5), one of the proposed downstream substrates of ERK3 and ERK4 was also activated in response to LPS, as revealed by the increased T182 phosphorylation of MK5 in LPS-treated HT-29 cells (Figure 2A and C).
evidence: Western blot (Figure 2A) and quantification (Figure 2C) demonstrate increased MK5 phosphorylation at T182 after LPS treatment.

claim: LPS does not significantly increase ERK3 mRNA levels in HT-29 cells.
source: Further, expression levels of ERK3 mRNA were determined with quantitative RT-PCR with no significant increase detected upon LPS treatment (Figure 2D).
evidence: RT-PCR data in Figure 2D shows no significant change in ERK3 mRNA after LPS treatment.

claim: LPS upregulates ERK3 protein levels in HT-29 cells without significantly increasing ERK3 protein half-life.
source: RT-PCR analyses coupled with cycloheximide (CHX) chase experiments revealed that LPS upregulates ERK3 protein levels (Figure 2E), while not exerting any significant increase in ERK3 protein half-life (Figure 2F).
evidence: CHX chase experiments (Figure 2E-F) show LPS increases ERK3 protein without affecting its degradation rate.

claim: LPS stimulation leads to a decrease in ERK3 protein levels in human colonic primary epithelial cells (HCPECs).
source: Interestingly, in these cells, LPS stimulation led to a decrease in the protein levels of ERK3, while activating MK5 and the classical MAPKs: ERK1/2 and p38 (Figure 2G–K).
evidence: Western blot (Figure 2G) and quantification (Figure 2H) show decreased ERK3 protein in HCPECs after LPS treatment.

claim: Primary epithelial cells express low levels of TLR4 compared to tumorigenic cells.
source: It has been reported that unlike the tumorigenic cells, primary epithelial cells express low levels of Toll-like receptor 4 (TLR4) (Cario and Podolsky, 2000; Pott and Hornef, 2012). This observation was confirmed in our cell culture models for HCPECs and HT-29 cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: RT-PCR data (Figure 2—figure supplement 2) confirms lower TLR4 expression in HCPECs compared to HT-29 cells, consistent with published literature.

claim: LPS treatment represses ERK3 ubiquitination in HT-29 cells.
source: Consistently, the polyubiquitination of endogenous ERK3 is modulated in response to LPS in both HT-29 cells and HCPEC: LPS treatment repressed and induced ERK3 ubiquitination in oncogenic and primary epithelial cells, respectively (Figure 2M and N, respectively).
evidence: Immunoprecipitation experiments (Figure 2M) show decreased ERK3 ubiquitination in HT-29 cells after LPS treatment.

claim: LPS treatment induces ERK3 ubiquitination in HCPECs.
source: Consistently, the polyubiquitination of endogenous ERK3 is modulated in response to LPS in both HT-29 cells and HCPEC: LPS treatment repressed and induced ERK3 ubiquitination in oncogenic and primary epithelial cells, respectively (Figure 2M and N, respectively).
evidence: Immunoprecipitation experiments (Figure 2N) show increased ERK3 ubiquitination in HCPECs after LPS treatment.

claim: ERK3 is required for the transcriptional regulation of CXCL8, CXCL10, CCL2 and CXCL6 in HCPECs.
source: In particular, we discovered that ERK3 is required for the transcriptional regulation of CXCL8, CXCL10, CCL2 and CXCL6 in HCPECs (Figure 4A).
evidence: RNA-seq data (Figure 4A) shows decreased expression of these chemokines in ERK3-depleted HCPECs.

claim: ERK3 regulates the mRNA levels of CXCL8, IL16 and CXCL6 in HCPECs.
source: Indeed, we validated that ERK3 regulates the mRNA levels of CXCL8, IL16 and CXCL6 in HCPECs (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: RT-PCR validation (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A-C) confirms ERK3-dependent regulation of these genes.

claim: IL-8 levels increase over time in HT-29 cells in response to LPS.
source: Interestingly, while IL-8 levels increased over time in HT-29 cells, drastic reduction in chemokine levels was observed in HCPECs upon LPS stimulation (Figure 4B and C, respectively).
evidence: ELISA data (Figure 4B) shows time-dependent increase in IL-8 in LPS-treated HT-29 cells.

claim: IL-8 levels decrease in HCPECs upon LPS stimulation.
source: Interestingly, while IL-8 levels increased over time in HT-29 cells, drastic reduction in chemokine levels was observed in HCPECs upon LPS stimulation (Figure 4B and C, respectively).
evidence: ELISA data (Figure 4C) shows decreased IL-8 in LPS-treated HCPECs.

claim: Depletion of ERK3 leads to a significant reduction in both basal and LPS-induced IL-8 levels in multiple cell lines.
source: Depletion of ERK3 with multiple siRNAs and shRNAs led to a significant reduction in both, basal as well as LPS-induced IL-8 levels, suggesting an obligatory role for ERK3 in the maintenance of IL-8 not only in HCPECs and HT-29 cells, but also in MDA-MB231 and HeLa cells (Figure 4D–F and Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: ELISA data from multiple cell lines (Figure 4D-F, Figure 4—figure supplement 2) shows reduced IL-8 upon ERK3 knockdown.

claim: CRISPR/Cas9 knockout of ERK3 reduces LPS-induced IL-8 levels in HT-29 cells.
source: Consistent with the observations made with si- and shRNAs, we affirmed that CRISPR/Cas9 knockout of ERK3 reduces LPS-induced IL-8 levels in CRISPR ERK3 HT-29 cells (Figure 4G–H).
evidence: ELISA data (Figure 4H) shows reduced IL-8 in ERK3 knockout HT-29 cells after LPS treatment.

claim: ERK3 is not required for the 3D growth of human gastric epithelium.
source: Data obtained from HGOs of two different patients revealed that ERK3 is not required for the 3D growth of human gastric epithelium as we failed to detect any significant change in the number or the size between the control (CRISPR Co) and ERK3-depleted (CRISPR ERK3) HGOs (Figure 4I–J).
evidence: Microscopy images (Figure 4I) and western blot (Figure 4J) show no morphological differences between control and ERK3 knockout HGOs.

claim: Knockout of ERK3 impairs IL-8 secretion in human gastric organoids.
source: However, consequently with the observations made for HCPECs, knockout of ERK3 impaired IL-8 secretion in human gastric organoids from two different patients (Figure 4K).
evidence: ELISA data (Figure 4K) shows reduced IL-8 in ERK3 knockout HGOs from two patients.

claim: Treatment with trametinib leads to a significant reduction of LPS-induced IL-8 levels in HT-29 cells.
source: Blocking of the MEK1/2-ERK1/2 pathway by trametinib led to a significant reduction of LPS-induced IL-8 levels in HT-29 cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 4A–B).
evidence: ELISA data (Figure 4—figure supplement 4B) shows decreased IL-8 in trametinib-treated HT-29 cells.

claim: Treatment with trametinib severely compromises ERK3 protein levels in HT-29 cells.
source: Interestingly, we observed that treatment with trametinib severely compromised protein levels of ERK3 in HT-29 cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 4A–B) with no significant effect on the ERK3 mRNA levels (Figure 4—figure supplement 4C).
evidence: Western blot (Figure 4—figure supplement 4A) and RT-PCR (Figure 4—figure supplement 4C) show decreased ERK3 protein but not mRNA after trametinib treatment.

claim: MG-132 treatment rescues ERK3 protein levels and IL-8 levels decreased by trametinib treatment in HT-29 cells.
source: Systemic block in proteasomal activity with MG-132 led to the accumulation of ERK3 protein and rescued IL-8 levels decreased by MEK inhibitor treatment in both, resting and LPS stimulated HT-29 cells despite inactive ERK1/2 (Figure 4—figure supplement 4D and E).
evidence: Western blot and ELISA data (Figure 4—figure supplement 4D-E) show MG-132 restores ERK3 and IL-8 levels in trametinib-treated cells.

claim: Endogenous MK5 positively regulates ERK3 expression.
source: Our observations indicate while endogenous MK5 positively regulates ERK3 expression, ERK4 exerts opposing effects on ERK3 protein levels (Figure 4—figure supplement 5).
evidence: Western blot data (Figure 4—figure supplement 5A) shows decreased ERK3 in MK5-depleted cells.

claim: ERK4 exerts opposing effects on ERK3 protein levels compared to MK5.
source: Our observations indicate while endogenous MK5 positively regulates ERK3 expression, ERK4 exerts opposing effects on ERK3 protein levels (Figure 4—figure supplement 5).
evidence: Western blot data (Figure 4—figure supplement 5C) shows increased ERK3 in ERK4-depleted cells.

claim: Expression of wild type ERK3 rescues IL-8 secretion in ERK3-depleted cells.
source: Interestingly, expression of WT as well as the kinase-dead version rescued the secretion of IL-8 in at least two different cell lines (Figure 5A–B).
evidence: ELISA data (Figure 5A-B) shows restored IL-8 levels in ERK3-depleted cells expressing wild type ERK3.

claim: Expression of kinase-dead ERK3 (K49A/K50A) rescues IL-8 secretion in ERK3-depleted cells.
source: Interestingly, expression of WT as well as the kinase-dead version rescued the secretion of IL-8 in at least two different cell lines (Figure 5A–B).
evidence: ELISA data (Figure 5A-B) shows restored IL-8 levels in ERK3-depleted cells expressing kinase-dead ERK3.

claim: ERK3 regulates IL-8 production in a kinase-independent manner.
source: Taken together, these results suggested a kinase-independent role for ERK3 in the regulation of IL-8 levels.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that both wild type and kinase-dead ERK3 rescue IL-8 production.

claim: Intravenous injection of ERK3-depleted MDA-MB231 cells results in fewer tumor lesions in the lungs compared to control cells.
source: Intravenous (i.v) injection of ERK3-depleted (shERK3) MDA-MB231 cells into the tail vein of immunocompromised mice resulted in less tumor lesions in the lungs and decreased pulmonary metastatic burden (Figure 5E and F, respectively and Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Histology quantification (Figure 5E) shows reduced number of lung tumors in mice injected with ERK3-depleted cells.

claim: Intravenous injection of ERK3-depleted MDA-MB231 cells results in decreased pulmonary metastatic burden compared to control cells.
source: Intravenous (i.v) injection of ERK3-depleted (shERK3) MDA-MB231 cells into the tail vein of immunocompromised mice resulted in less tumor lesions in the lungs and decreased pulmonary metastatic burden (Figure 5E and F, respectively and Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Histology quantification (Figure 5F) shows reduced tumor burden in lungs of mice injected with ERK3-depleted cells.

claim: Depletion of ERK3 reduces IL-8 promoter activity in MDA-MB231 cells.
source: Gaussia Luciferase (GLuc) promoter reporter assay revealed that the depletion of ERK3 with siRNAs reduced IL-8 promoter activity and consistently IL-8 production in the same cells (Figure 6A–C).
evidence: Luciferase assay data (Figure 6B) shows decreased IL-8 promoter activity in ERK3-depleted cells.

claim: ERK3 is required for the activation of AP-1 transcription factor in HCPECs.
source: Our results highlighted AP-1 as one of the TFs positively regulated by ERK3 in HCPECs (Figure 6E and Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Transcription factor activity assay (Figure 6E) shows decreased AP-1 activity in ERK3-depleted HCPECs.

claim: NF-κB activity is increased in ERK3-depleted HCPECs.
source: Interestingly, in contrast to AP-1, NF-κB activity was increased in the ERK3-depleted HCPECs (Figure 6—figure supplement 3), further implicating AP-1 as the transcription factor primarily contributing to IL-8 in response to ERK3 depletion under these settings (Figure 6E–F).
evidence: Transcription factor profiling assay (Figure 6—figure supplement 3A) shows increased NF-κB activity in ERK3-depleted cells.

claim: LPS-induced AP-1 activity in HT-29 cells is impaired by ERK3 knockout.
source: AP-1 TF filter plate assay revealed that LPS-induced AP-1 DNA binding activity and IL-8 production are dependent on ERK3 protein levels (Figure 6G–H).
evidence: Transcription factor activity assay (Figure 6G) shows reduced AP-1 activity in ERK3 knockout HT-29 cells after LPS treatment.

claim: ERK3 forms a complex with c-Jun upon LPS stimulation in HT-29 cells.
source: We detected a complex formation between these two proteins upon LPS stimulation in cells by performing two-way immunoprecipitation (IP) assays with validated antibodies directed against both c-Jun and ERK3 antigens (Figure 7A).
evidence: Co-immunoprecipitation experiments (Figure 7A) show ERK3-c-Jun interaction after LPS treatment.

claim: ERK3 and c-Jun protein levels increase upon LPS stimulation in HT-29 cells.
source: Cell fractionation and immunofluorescence (IF) studies confirmed that while total ERK3 and c-Jun protein levels increase upon LPS stimulation, a significant fraction of ERK3 can be detected in the nuclear compartments, ultimately leading to an enhanced nuclear abundance of c-Jun protein upon stimulation (Figure 7B–D and Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Western blot (Figure 7C) and immunofluorescence (Figure 7B) show increased ERK3 and c-Jun after LPS treatment.

claim: A significant fraction of ERK3 can be detected in the nuclear compartments upon LPS stimulation.
source: Cell fractionation and immunofluorescence (IF) studies confirmed that while total ERK3 and c-Jun protein levels increase upon LPS stimulation, a significant fraction of ERK3 can be detected in the nuclear compartments, ultimately leading to an enhanced nuclear abundance of c-Jun protein upon stimulation (Figure 7B–D and Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Cell fractionation (Figure 7—figure supplement 1) and immunofluorescence (Figure 7B) show nuclear ERK3 after LPS treatment.

claim: ERK3 and c-Jun show significant nuclear co-localization in HT-29 cells.
source: Further, single-cell level analyses revealed a significant nuclear co-localization between ERK3 and c-Jun proteins in both control and LPS stimulated HT-29 cells with Pearson's correlation coefficient PCC: 0.9172 ± 0.0098 and PCC: 0.9237 ± 0.01 for control and LPS stimulated cells, respectively (mean ± SEM) (Figure 7E).
evidence: Co-localization analysis (Figure 7E) shows high Pearson's correlation coefficient for ERK3 and c-Jun in the nucleus.

claim: Knockdown of ERK3 reduces LPS-induced nuclear abundance of c-Jun in HT-29 cells.
source: Knockdown of ERK3 expectedly abolished the observed nuclear co-localization (Figure 7B and E) and interestingly further reduced LPS-induced nuclear abundance of c-Jun (Figure 7B and F).
evidence: Immunofluorescence (Figure 7B) and quantification (Figure 7F) show reduced nuclear c-Jun in ERK3-depleted cells.

claim: Depletion of ERK3 in epithelial cells leads to a significant reduction in the chemotaxis of THP1 cells in vitro.
source: Transwell migration experiments involving THP1 cells and human neutrophils revealed that depletion of ERK3 in the epithelial cells leads to a significant reduction in the chemotaxis of these leukocytes (Figure 8A–B).
evidence: Transwell migration assay (Figure 8B) shows reduced THP1 migration toward ERK3-depleted cell supernatants.

claim: Depletion of ERK3 in epithelial cells leads to a significant reduction in the chemotaxis of human neutrophils in vitro.
source: Transwell migration experiments involving THP1 cells and human neutrophils revealed that depletion of ERK3 in the epithelial cells leads to a significant reduction in the chemotaxis of these leukocytes (Figure 8A–B).
evidence: Transwell migration assay (Figure 8A) shows reduced neutrophil migration toward ERK3-depleted cell supernatants.

claim: Injection of supernatants from ERK3-depleted HCPECs results in significantly reduced migration of granulocytes to the intraperitoneal cavity in mice.
source: Consistent with the observations we made in vitro, injection of the supernatants obtained from ERK3-depleted HCPECs (siERK3 supernatant) resulted in significantly reduced migration of granulocytes and monocytes to the intraperitoneal cavity in comparison to the controls (Figure 8D–E), while not exerting any significant effect on the lymphocytes recruitment (Figure 8F).
evidence: In vivo chemotaxis assay (Figure 8D) shows reduced granulocyte recruitment after injection of ERK3-depleted cell supernatants.

claim: Injection of supernatants from ERK3-depleted HCPECs results in significantly reduced migration of monocytes to the intraperitoneal cavity in mice.
source: Consistent with the observations we made in vitro, injection of the supernatants obtained from ERK3-depleted HCPECs (siERK3 supernatant) resulted in significantly reduced migration of granulocytes and monocytes to the intraperitoneal cavity in comparison to the controls (Figure 8D–E), while not exerting any significant effect on the lymphocytes recruitment (Figure 8F).
evidence: In vivo chemotaxis assay (Figure 8E) shows reduced monocyte recruitment after injection of ERK3-depleted cell supernatants.

claim: IL-8 neutralizing antibody decreases the migration of neutrophils toward epithelial cell supernatants.
source: As shown in Figure 8A and B, the presence of the IL-8 antibody decreased the migration of neutrophils and THP1 cells.
evidence: Transwell migration assay (Figure 8A) shows reduced neutrophil migration in the presence of IL-8 neutralizing antibody.

claim: IL-8 neutralizing antibody decreases the migration of THP1 cells toward epithelial cell supernatants.
source: As shown in Figure 8A and B, the presence of the IL-8 antibody decreased the migration of neutrophils and THP1 cells.
evidence: Transwell migration assay (Figure 8B) shows reduced THP1 migration in the presence of IL-8 neutralizing antibody.

claim: Intraperitoneal injection of human recombinant IL-8 into mice significantly attracts leukocytes.
source: As expected, intraperitoneal injection of human recombinant IL-8 into mice significantly attracted leukocytes confirming the crucial role for IL-8 in this process (Figure 8D–F).
evidence: In vivo chemotaxis assay (Figure 8D-F) shows increased leukocyte recruitment after injection of recombinant IL-8.

claim: ERK3 positively regulates ICAM-1 mRNA expression in HCPECs.
source: Interestingly, in addition to IL-8, ERK3 also positively regulates ICAM-1 mRNA expression as revealed by the RNAseq analysis (Figure 8—figure supplement 1).
evidence: RNA-seq data (Figure 8—figure supplement 1) shows decreased ICAM-1 expression in ERK3-depleted HCPECs.

claim: Genetic deletion of ERK3 led to respiratory failure, disturbed growth and neonatal lethality in mice within the first days of life.
source: It was reported that genetic deletion of ERK3 led to a respiratory failure, disturbed growth and neonatal lethality in mice within the first days of life; however, these observations were recently challenged by two publications that confirmed that the observed phenotype was probably attributed to off target effects (Klinger et al., 2009; Ronkina et al., 2019; Soulez et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is based on published literature cited in the text.

claim: The observed phenotype of neonatal lethality in ERK3 knockout mice was probably attributed to off target effects.
source: It was reported that genetic deletion of ERK3 led to a respiratory failure, disturbed growth and neonatal lethality in mice within the first days of life; however, these observations were recently challenged by two publications that confirmed that the observed phenotype was probably attributed to off target effects (Klinger et al., 2009; Ronkina et al., 2019; Soulez et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is based on recent publications that challenged earlier findings.

claim: ERK3 possesses a single phospho-acceptor site at serine 189 within its N-terminus domain.
source: Unlike conventional MAPKs, ERK3 possesses a single phospho-acceptor site at serine 189 within its N-terminus domain, which is constitutively phosphorylated in resting cells.
evidence: This is a known characteristic of ERK3 based on established scientific knowledge.

claim: ERK3 is a highly unstable protein with a half-life of 30 to 45 min.
source: ERK3 is a highly unstable protein with a half-life of 30 to 45 min that undergoes N-terminal ubiquitination.
evidence: This is established knowledge about ERK3 protein stability.

claim: Usp20 was identified as the first deubiquitinating enzyme (DUB) for ERK3.
source: However, Usp20 was recently identified as the first deubiquitinating enzyme (DUB) for ERK3 (Mathien et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is based on published literature cited in the text.

claim: IL-8 is one of the first chemokines released by injured or inflamed epithelium.
source: IL-8 is one of the first chemokines released by injured or inflamed epithelium, and it is constitutively expressed by intestinal epithelial cells (Eckmann et al., 1993).
evidence: This claim is based on published literature cited in the text.

claim: Transcriptional activation of the IL-8 promoter strictly relies on the binding of inducible transcription factors such as NF-κB and AP-1.
source: Transcriptional activation of the IL-8 promoter strictly relies on the binding of inducible transcription factors (TFs) such as NF-κB and activating protein 1 (AP-1) (Hoffmann et al., 2002; Jundi and Greene, 2015).
evidence: This claim is based on published literature cited in the text.

claim: High levels of IL-8 are a poor prognostic factor in melanoma, breast, liver, lung and colon cancer.
source: High levels of this chemokine are a poor prognostic factor in melanoma, breast, liver, lung and colon cancer (David et al., 2016; Ueda et al., 1994).
evidence: This claim is based on published literature cited in the text.

claim: IL-8 has been reported to enhance migration and metastasis of breast carcinoma cells MDA-MB231.
source: Similarly, IL-8 has been reported to enhance migration and thus metastasis of breast carcinoma cells MDA-MB231, which also carry a KRAS G13D mutation (Jayatilaka et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is based on published literature cited in the text.

claim: MDA-MB231 cells carry a KRAS G13D mutation.
source: Similarly, IL-8 has been reported to enhance migration and thus metastasis of breast carcinoma cells MDA-MB231, which also carry a KRAS G13D mutation (Jayatilaka et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is based on published literature cited in the text.

claim: c-Jun can translocate and be retained in the nucleus as a monomer, without binding to its target sequence.
source: The AP-1 transcription factor c-Jun can translocate and be retained in the nucleus as a monomer, without binding to its target sequence (Karin, 1996; Schreck et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is based on published literature cited in the text.

claim: Nuclear translocation of c-Jun is independent of its phosphorylation by and interaction with JNK.
source: Although c-Jun is predominantly regulated by JNK it was demonstrated that its nuclear translocation is independent of its phosphorylation by and interaction with JNK (Schreck et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is based on published literature cited in the text.

claim: ERK3 has been shown to be constitutively localized to both cytoplasmic and nuclear compartments.
source: ERK3 has already been reported to be constitutively localized to both, cytoplasmic and nuclear compartments (Julien et al., 2003), but its subcellular localization has been shown not to be affected by any of the common MAPKs activating stimuli (Julien et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is based on published literature cited in the text.

claim: Subcellular localization of ERK3 has been shown not to be affected by common MAPKs activating stimuli.
source: ERK3 has already been reported to be constitutively localized to both, cytoplasmic and nuclear compartments (Julien et al., 2003), but its subcellular localization has been shown not to be affected by any of the common MAPKs activating stimuli (Julien et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is based on published literature cited in the text, though the authors' data suggests LPS does affect ERK3 localization.

claim: LPS stimulation triggers the accumulation of ERK3 protein in both cytoplasm and nucleus of HT-29 cells.
source: Here, we demonstrate that LPS stimulation triggers the accumulation of ERK3 protein, resulting in its enhanced expression in both, cytoplasm and nucleus (Figure 7B–D and Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Immunofluorescence (Figure 7B-D) and cell fractionation (Figure 7—figure supplement 1) show increased ERK3 in both compartments after LPS treatment.

claim: Mice lack the IL-8 encoding gene.
source: Importantly, although mice lack the IL-8 encoding gene, they do express a receptor analogous to human CXCR2, which in response to human IL-8 mediates neutrophil chemotaxis (Singer and Sansonetti, 2004).
evidence: This claim is based on published literature cited in the text.

claim: Mice express a receptor analogous to human CXCR2, which in response to human IL-8 mediates neutrophil chemotaxis.
source: Importantly, although mice lack the IL-8 encoding gene, they do express a receptor analogous to human CXCR2, which in response to human IL-8 mediates neutrophil chemotaxis (Singer and Sansonetti, 2004).
evidence: This claim is based on published literature cited in the text.

claim: IL-8 upregulates ICAM-1 in HT-29 cells, promoting neutrophil-epithelium cell adhesion.
source: Previous studies showed that IL-8 upregulates intercellular adhesion molecule-1 (ICAM-1) in HT-29 cells, thus promoting neutrophil-epithelium cell adhesion (Kelly et al., 1994).
evidence: This claim is based on published literature cited in the text.

claim: Secreted IL-8 enhances the expression of CD11/CD18 adhesion receptors by neutrophils.
source: Moreover, studies on epithelial cells revealed that secreted IL-8 enhances the expression of CD11/CD18 adhesion receptors by neutrophils, which enables the migration by promoting the interaction of the receptors with ICAM-1 (Kelly et al., 1994).
evidence: This claim is based on published literature cited in the text.

claim: Upregulation of TLR4 is associated with inflammatory bowel diseases like ulcerative colitis.
source: Interestingly, upregulation of TLR4 is associated with inflammatory bowel diseases like ulcerative colitis (Cario and Podolsky, 2000; Fan and Liu, 2015; Tang et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is based on published literature cited in the text.

claim: TLR4 is upregulated in colorectal cancer, including HT-29 cells.
source: Moreover, observed discrepancies in responsiveness to LPS between colon carcinoma and primary epithelial cells can be further explained by previous studies describing upregulation of TLR4 in colorectal cancer, including HT-29 cells (Abreu et al., 2002; Furrie et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is based on published literature cited in the text.

claim: LPS-TLR4 signaling results in tumor progression and metastasis.
source: Published observations indicate that LPS-TLR4 signaling results in tumor progression and metastasis (Gross et al., 1995; Tang et al., 2010; Yesudhas et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is based on published literature cited in the text.

claim: Low expression of TLR4 by HCPECs might explain why they can tolerate LPS and maintain hyporesponsiveness toward luminal bacteria.
source: Intestinal epithelium is constantly exposed to significant levels of luminal LPS and the low expression of TLR4 by HCPECs might provide an explanation why they can tolerate LPS and maintain hyporesponsiveness toward luminal bacteria (Otte et al., 2004).
evidence: This is a speculation based on the observed low TLR4 expression in HCPECs and published literature.

claim: ERK3 is critically required for basal as well as LPS-induced IL-8 levels in both primary and tumor cells.
source: However, ERK3 is critically required for basal as well as LPS-induced IL-8 levels in both primary and tumor cells.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on multiple experimental observations presented in the manuscript.

claim: ERK3 controls the transcription factor AP-1/c-Jun in both HCPECs and HT-29 cells.
source: Intriguingly, the effect is kinase-independent and we demonstrated that ERK3 controls the transcription factor AP-1/c-Jun in both, HCPECs and HT-29 cells (Figure 6D–E and Figure 6G, respectively).
evidence: Transcription factor activity assays (Figure 6D-E, 6G) show ERK3-dependent regulation of AP-1 in both cell types.

claim: ERK3-AP-1 activity directly correlates with IL-8 levels in both normal and transformed cells.
source: We further observed that ERK3-AP-1 activity directly correlates with IL-8 levels in both normal and transformed cells (Figure 6E–F and G–H, respectively).
evidence: Parallel measurements of AP-1 activity and IL-8 levels (Figure 6E-F, 6G-H) show correlation in both cell types.

claim: ERK3 is required for nuclear abundance of c-Jun protein.
source: Our studies revealed that ERK3 is required for nuclear abundance of c-Jun protein (Figure 7B and F).
evidence: Immunofluorescence (Figure 7B) and quantification (Figure 7F) show reduced nuclear c-Jun in ERK3-depleted cells.

claim: ERK3 interacts with c-Jun and regulates the DNA-binding activity of AP-1.
source: We provide evidence that ERK3 interacts with c-Jun and regulates the DNA-binding activity of AP-1 (Figure 6D–E and G and Figure 7) which might reflect a non-catalytic scaffolding function described for other kinases as well (Rauch et al., 2011).
evidence: Co-immunoprecipitation (Figure 7A) and transcription factor activity assays (Figure 6D-E, 6G) demonstrate ERK3-c-Jun interaction and AP-1 regulation.

claim: JNK controls c-Jun activity by sub-nuclear localization of AP-1 proteins.
source: Nevertheless, JNK controls c-Jun activity by sub-nuclear localization of AP-1 proteins (Gazon et al., 2017), therefore it is tempting to propose ERK3 as a novel MAPK required for the nuclear abundance of c-Jun.
evidence: This claim is based on published literature cited in the text.

claim: Loss of ERK3 inhibits IL-8 production despite the activation of classical MAPKs and NF-κB.
source: Furthermore, we consistently observed that loss of ERK3 inhibited IL-8 production and secretion in multiple cell types - despite the activation of classical MAPKs and NF-κB.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on multiple experimental observations presented in the manuscript.

claim: LPS stimulation led to a downregulation of NF-κB activity in ERK3-depleted HCPECs.
source: Worth mentioning is that LPS stimulation led to a downregulation of NF-κB activity in ERK3-depleted cells (Figure 6—figure supplement 3A), which surprisingly had no additive effect on neither protein (Figure 6F) nor mRNA (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A) levels of CXCL8/IL-8.
evidence: Transcription factor profiling assay (Figure 6—figure supplement 3A) shows decreased NF-κB activity in ERK3-depleted cells after LPS treatment.

claim: Inhibition of MEK1 with trametinib reduces the protein stability of ERK3.
source: We were able to observe that inhibition of MEK1 with trametinib reduces the protein stability of ERK3 and thus the published results claiming a unique role for the classical MAPK in the production of IL-8 needs to be evaluated with caution.
evidence: This is based on the observation that trametinib treatment decreases ERK3 protein levels (Figure 4—figure supplement 4A).

claim: ERK3 plays an obligatory and synergistic role with classical MAPKs in mediating LPS-induced chemokines.
source: Our data suggest an obligatory and synergistic role for ERK3 in mediating LPS-induced chemokines.
evidence: This is a summary interpretation based on the experimental data showing ERK3 is required for IL-8 production even when classical MAPKs are active.

claim: ERK3 interacts with c-Jun and regulates AP-1 activity, which directly contributes to high basal and LPS-mediated IL-8 levels in HCPECs and HT-29 cells.
source: While verifying the role of ERK3 in the regulation of CXCL8/IL-8, we uncover that ERK3 interacts with c-Jun and regulates AP-1 activity, which directly contributes to the high basal and LPS-mediated IL-8 levels in HCPECs and HT-29 cells, respectively.
evidence: This is a summary statement integrating multiple experimental findings from the manuscript.

claim: The decrease in expression of ERK3 directly correlates with IL-8 levels in both HCPECs and HT-29 cells.
